error.message: Beam ran out of room before finishing its answer. Trying again may work.

lines.text: Do you know I was once not very far from seeing--really seeing you?
lines.note: Your first letter's nearly-seen-you memory opens the whole longing.

lines.text: Real warm Spring, dear Miss Barrett, and the birds know it; and in Spring I shall see you, surely see you--for when did I once fail to get whatever I had set my heart upon?
lines.note: Spring promise to see her, echoing that first near-miss.

lines.text: Yes, but, dear Mr. Browning, I want the spring according to the new 'style' (mine), and not the old one of you and the rest of the poets.
lines.note: Her playful answer about spring in her own style, answering your promise.

lines.text: I have but one greater delight in the world than in hearing from you.
lines.note: Later letter where hearing from her is second only to seeing her.

lines.text: I mean such truths as may be painful to me though truths....
lines.note: Her reply that you could write from the end of the world, answering your delight in hearing from her.

lines.text: My only good in this world--that against which all the world goes for nothing--is to spend my life with you, and be yours.
lines.note: Late declaration that your only good is to spend life with her.

lines.text: Let it be this way, ever dearest.
lines.note: Her acceptance of your will as duty and desire.

lines.text: Yet I shall see you on Monday, and shall watch and wait as those who wait for the morning ... that is, the Monday-morning!
lines.note: Her watch-and-wait line for Monday morning.

lines.text: Now, dearest, somehow I can’t write the great proof down—I will tell you on Monday—as to my good sense.
lines.note: Your promise to tell her the proof you cannot write down.

lines.text: Well,—and this is what I meant to say from the beginning of the letter, I love your inability to feel it in spite of right and justice and rationality.
lines.note: Your offer to give back her golden words.
